title: The Notebooks in the River
hook: a grocer is told to drown his songs, and does
carry: God hears the language of home
tomorrow: Why would a weaver lie down where his teacher would step?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tukaram split the last broken stalk of sugarcane with his wife. One for you, one for me.
screen: `TUKARAM.` · `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: On the bank of the Indrayani, a man holds a bundle of handwritten notebooks full of songs. He steps to the edge and lets them go. They sink into the brown water and are gone. Nobody stole them or tore them up. He was told to do this, and he did it himself. Then he sits down on the bare ground by the water, and he doesn't get up.
screen: `A BUNDLE OF NOTEBOOKS.` → `INTO THE RIVER.` → `HE SITS DOWN ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: The songs are abhangs, the short devotional verses of the Varkari saints, made to be sung in Marathi, the everyday language Jnaneshwar had already opened the Gita in. Tukaram made them for Vitthal, and people sang them. Not everyone was pleased. Tradition names a learned man, Rameshwar Bhatt, who objected that a grocer had no business composing songs about sacred things, and in everyday Marathi at that. The story says he ordered Tukaram to sink his notebooks in the river. And Tukaram did. He doesn't argue, hide a copy, or run to another town. He obeys, then sits on the bank and refuses food, turning it all over to Vitthal. If the songs were his, let them drown. If they were Vitthal's, let Vitthal decide. Days go by. Then, tradition says, the notebooks rose to the surface of the Indrayani, dry. The story goes one step further: the man who gave the order fell ill, and was healed only after he came to Tukaram and became his follower. It isn't told as a victory over an enemy, but as two people both changed by the songs. Here is the teaching. For centuries much sacred learning was kept in Sanskrit, by the learned. The bhakti saints sang to God in the languages their mothers spoke, Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, and their songs teach that God hears those just as well. Varkaris still sing Tukaram's abhangs. In the season of the great walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, a palanquin carrying his sandals sets out from Dehu, and the pilgrims sing his Marathi words along the road.
screen: `ABHANGS, IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `SINK THEM IN THE RIVER.` · `THE NOTEBOOKS RISE.` · then, large: `GOD HEARS THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.`

segments.voice: Pick one short prayer or line you already know: a mantra, a line from a bhajan, a grace before meals. Say it once as you learned it. Then say what it means in your own everyday language, slowly, as if speaking to someone right beside you. That's what Tukaram's abhangs did. If you don't pray, say the words you'd most want someone to hear, in your own tongue.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who sank his songs in the Indrayani when he was told to, and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose.
Your line: God hears the language of home. Tukaram's Marathi songs went into the river and, tradition says, came back up. That's day nine hundred twenty.
